items: A session in a drive, your home folder, Downloads, Desktop, Documents or OneDrive no longer spends 20 seconds trying to snapshot it before giving up: Rewind is off there from the start, said once in a quiet note instead of an orange warning.

0.6.37 and 0.6.39 were built apart; this version has both. Coming from 0.6.39, you gain 0.6.37's fixes: new files can be written on exFAT and FAT32 drives, a dropped connection is retried and can move on to your backup model, Retry is no longer blocked for ten minutes after a model left a provider's list, provider errors read as sentences, and Graft does less work while it is minimized. Coming from 0.6.37, you gain 0.6.39's visual pass, below.

The cards, bars and message box under a conversation line up with it at every window size. They used to stick out on the right, where the conversation keeps room for its scrollbar. The turn marks at the top left no longer touch the text in a narrow window.

A list that goes on past an edge fades out there, so a row that is cut off reads as more to scroll to: the home screen above the message box, and both columns of Settings, where About was hidden below Data. In a narrow side panel the Changes, Files, Search and Problems tabs scroll instead of running under the close button.
On the home screen every session title starts in the same place. Whether a session needs you, stopped on an error or is running is shown after its title.

An edited file shows only the side that changed: a new file reads +44, without a red −0 beside it. What you picked in a menu or a list is checked in your accent color, and the model filter reads “Filter 1 model” when there is one.

Writing a new file works on drives without hard links, such as an exFAT or FAT32 USB drive or a second drive formatted that way. Before, every new file on such a drive failed with EISDIR; a file someone else creates in the meantime is still never overwritten.

A reply whose connection the server drops before anything arrives is retried like any other network failure, and can move on to your backup model. It used to end the turn with an unexplained "terminated".
A model that a provider's list left out for a while no longer blocks Retry: Graft asks the provider again before refusing the turn, and goes ahead if the model is back.
Provider errors read as sentences: "Rate limited (429): Too Many Requests" instead of the JSON the provider sent, and OpenRouter's "Provider returned error" now says which provider refused and why.

Less work in the background: the status bar stops checking the folder's changes while Graft is minimized or covered, and stops asking at all where Git is not installed; the Browser panel stops probing for dev servers while it can't be seen. Scrolling a long conversation works out the current turn once a frame instead of on every scroll event.

Two sessions at once. Open beside, from a session's menu, puts another session next to the open one, with a handle between them to drag the width. The pane you last clicked or typed in is the one the keyboard belongs to, so Ctrl+F and Esc act on that session only. A button closes the conversation beside.

Sessions you file away. Move to group files a session under a name of your own; the groups are sections in the sidebar, and they can be renamed or removed without losing the sessions in them. Mark as completed takes a session out of the working lists and puts it under Completed, where the same filters apply. Writing to it again marks it in progress and it comes back where it was.
Find steps through the matches with F3 and Shift+F3, from anywhere in the window, and Copy as Markdown from a session's menu puts the conversation on the clipboard without a save dialog.

A model on your computer is measured against the context its server loaded, not the length it was trained for: llama.cpp and LM Studio are asked what they hold. Local servers get up to 15 minutes to read a long prompt, and Ollama keeps a model loaded for 30 minutes between turns, unless OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE sets another time.

Models whose server has no tool support can use tools: Graft describes the tools in the prompt and reads the calls the model writes as text, in the Hermes, Qwen and Mistral forms. A call a local model writes as text in a normal reply is run too, and when a server refuses tools, Graft switches that model to text until Graft restarts.

A local model whose window is known to be 64K or less (its server reports it, you set it in Settings, or it runs in Ollama) gets a lean code prompt, with the same safety rules, your personalization and the site brief, and the core tools (Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, Shell and the like). The others are one ToolSearch away.
Settings → Providers → Find servers on this computer finds Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM, Jan and KoboldCpp on their usual ports and adds one in a click. The first-run setup offers it too.
Settings → Models: a custom model can choose its prompt (Automatic, Full or Lean) and how it calls tools (Automatic, Native or Written in text).
A model a provider doesn’t serve is named in the message, which says to pick another model or refresh the list in Settings → Models.

A GEMINI.md file counts as project notes when a folder has no GRAFT.md, AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md. The project’s .cursor/rules files marked alwaysApply are read too, or its .cursorrules file when there are none, and a rule that can’t be read is skipped.

Deleting a session works again after a large folder was being snapshotted: Graft now stops the whole git it started (on Windows the git on PATH starts a second one, which kept running and held the session’s files), and a delete never fails on that folder.
Replies start sooner in large folders: the snapshot Rewind needs is taken while the model starts answering, and only a change to a file waits for it.

Settings → Models has a section for each kind of media model your providers offer: images, video, voices, music and transcription. OpenRouter’s are listed by kind, OpenAI’s and Google’s too, and the well-known ones on other servers. Use makes one the model for images, video or Read aloud.

Graft makes video. GenerateVideo turns a prompt, or a picture of your project, into a clip with OpenRouter’s video models (Veo, Seedance, Kling, Wan, Hailuo and more) and saves it in the project. Pick the model in Settings → Models.

54 integrations to add in one step, 42 of them new: ElevenLabs for game sound; Figma files, shadcn/ui, Chrome DevTools, Next.js, Svelte, Astro and Webflow for interfaces; DeepWiki, Microsoft Learn, AWS and Cloudflare docs, Netlify, Render, Stripe, PostHog, Semgrep, CircleCI and Kubernetes for developers; Supabase, Neon, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis and DuckDB for data; Hugging Face, arXiv, paper search, Wikipedia, Zotero, Perplexity, Exa, Brave Search, Firecrawl and Tavily for research; Jira and Confluence, Asana, Airtable, Memory and Sequential thinking. A search finds them.

Sending and deleting work in any folder again. Your message shows the moment you send it; the snapshot Rewind needs is taken after it, and is given up with a note when a folder (a whole Downloads folder, say) takes longer than 20 seconds. Stop and Delete end a turn at once, wherever it has got to, and messages sent one after another all arrive, in order, even while the one before is still on its way.
A turn stopped before the model said a word says "Stopped." under your message, as a reply cut short does.
Slim scrollbars: rounded, faint until you point at them or scroll, brighter while you scroll and tinted while you drag.

Connectors show the apps they reach. Roblox Studio, Blender, Figma, GitHub, Linear, Notion and about fifty more get their own icon and name, and a server that names itself and sends an icon is shown by those. In the details column a connector opens to where it runs, its version, its tools, Reconnect and Open in Customize; Customize and the steps of a turn show the same icons.
A right-click on the details column chooses which of its cards it shows.
Open a file (Ctrl+P) opens a file that matches what you typed, however quickly you press Enter.

A code session has a details column at its right: where it runs (this computer, the folder, the worktree, the branch), what fills its context part by part with the free space and how far automatic compaction is, your MCP connectors with Reconnect and Sign in, the files it made, its background commands and agents with live times, and its changes with Review and Create PR. It takes the panels' place and comes back when they close; the button at the top right shows and hides it.

3D models open in Graft. A .glb, .gltf, .obj, .stl, .fbx or .ply file shows in the Files panel as a model you can turn, zoom and move, in wireframe or not, with its animations playing. When a reply names a model file, say one Blender just exported, the turn ends with the model drawn in the conversation.
Pictures a tool sends back, a render from Blender or a capture of Roblox Studio, show as thumbnails on its row and open large.

Several queued messages fold into one line, "3 messages queued · Next: …", that opens to the list, with Clear all. At Max and Taproot a short note above the message box says what the level costs, until you close it.

Settings → Appearance → Code colors: a theme for code while Graft is dark and one while it is light, among Vitesse, GitHub, Catppuccin, Night Owl, One, Tokyo Night, Dracula, Rosé Pine, Everforest, Gruvbox, Nord, Monokai, Solarized and Min, each previewed live.
The Terminal panel's menu sets the cursor, copy on select and how many lines are kept, and clears the terminal. The Changes panel's menu wraps long lines and can hide changes of whitespace alone.

Settings → Permissions gains limits that hold across turns: tokens and cost for a whole session, for a whole project (every session in its folder) and for a day (everything used on this computer today). Reaching one pauses the turn with the number it reached and a Continue button, like the limits for one turn.

The Changes panel's Search tab can compose a replace: press Ask Graft to replace the matches, type what they should become, and press it again. The request is written into your message box with the search as it ran and what it found. Nothing is sent and nothing is replaced by the tab: the turn that follows makes the change, with its checkpoint and its diff.

Tokens read from a provider's cache count at a tenth, as they are billed, and a model with no published price is named once and counted in tokens only. A chat belongs to no folder, so it is not counted against a project.

The Changes panel has a Search tab: every line of the project that holds what you type, under its file, with the matches marked. Ctrl+Shift+H opens it with the text you had selected in the box. Match case, whole words or a regular expression, and say which files to look in or leave out. A line opens its file in the editor at the match, and the results can go to your message.

The Browser panel checks a page. Check the page lists text that is hard to read with its contrast, pictures, buttons and fields without a name, headings out of order, small targets crowded together, and a layout wider than its window. Press a finding to see it in the page. Ask Graft to fix these writes the request for you to send.
One press sends the page as a phone, a tablet and a desktop lay it out to your message, whatever size the panel is. An element you pick arrives with a picture of itself, for a model that can see.
Graft checks its own pages the same way. When it builds a site or tests an app in the browser it runs the check at a phone's and a desktop's width, and it can take its screenshots at any width.

Fixed: Esc in the Settings search emptied the box and closed Settings with it. It now empties the box, and the next Esc closes Settings. A screenshot Graft took while the Browser panel was shut no longer hangs.

Sites can be real projects. Choose React + TypeScript beside a new site's name and Graft starts it as one: components in .tsx files, strict types, styles in modules, built with Vite. It is what a new site starts on when Node.js is installed.

Graft asks before it installs a site's packages and before a build, as it does for any command. The preview shows what the build made, reloads after every build, and keeps the last good page when a build fails. The type check is the project's check.
Plain HTML is still there for a site with no build and nothing to install, and the sites you already have stay as they are. The gallery says which kind each site is.

Type /btw and a question to ask something on the side, also while Graft is working. The answer appears above the message box, written from the conversation so far. Neither the question nor the answer is added to the conversation: Graft does not see them, now or later.

Graft moves more. A page you open rises into place while the sidebar holds still, windows and menus spring open, and a message you send travels up from the message box. A panel comes in from its edge, also when it joins others.
Settings → Appearance → Motion style chooses between Lively and Calm. Calm is the short fades of 0.6.27. With Motion on Reduced, or a system that asks for less motion, nothing moves in either.
Settings opens as a window over what you were doing, and Esc puts you back there. The session underneath keeps working.
Changing page, session, theme or transcript view cross-fades instead of cutting.
The panel column slides open and shut, and the conversation moves aside with it.
A session that moves in the sidebar, into Needs you or to the top after a reply, travels to its new place.
A task that finishes shows it as it happens.
A menu opened inside a dialog is drawn over it, not behind it.
If Graft looks still, Windows may have animations turned off: Settings → Appearance → Motion → On animates Graft anyway.

Comment on any line of a diff, in the Changes panel or under an edit in the conversation, or on a line or selection in the editor (Ctrl+Alt+M, or the button above it). Your comments wait above the message box and go to Graft with your next message, each with its file, its line and the code it is about.
Ctrl+P opens a file by typing part of its name; add :42 to land on a line. Ctrl+T finds a function, class or type by name in a trusted TypeScript or JavaScript project.

The Changes panel has a Problems tab: the errors and warnings in the files you have changed, from the built-in language server, each opening at its place. Ask Graft to fix these writes the request into the message box for you to send.
A file named in a reply opens that file. Click src/app.ts:42 and the Files panel shows it in the editor at that line. Each file on the edited-files card has Open as well.
Code blocks say which file they are for and how long they are. A block of more than 40 lines shows its first 20 until you open it, and Wrap lines wraps it. Copy still copies all of the code.
A one-line shell command has a button that types it into the terminal. Graft never runs it: you press Enter.
Ctrl+F finds text in the conversation you are in. Enter and Shift+Enter step through the matches, and Esc closes it.
Equations are set as equations. Prices and shell variables are left as they are.
A Mermaid block has Draw this, which asks Graft to redraw it as a proper diagram.

While a picture is being made, a grid of dots stands in for it: a line of bright dots walks the grid from one green dot to the next, and the corner shows the time so far or what the engine last said. The line above reads “Creating image”.
A picture that has just been made comes into focus instead of popping in. One picture shows large, at its own shape. Click any generated picture to see it in a viewer with zoom (+, −, 0 to fit).
An SVG the model writes shows as the drawing once its code is complete. The button beside Copy switches between the drawing and its code.
While Graft searches the web, the line above the steps counts what it has found: “Searching 12 websites”.

Sources show the picture a page offers for itself, when a page that was read has one. Graft fetches it the way it fetches site icons: from public https addresses, without cookies, and re-encoded before it is shown. Pages read before this version have none.
In a chat, a quoted block in a reply is a card of its own, so a key fact or a caveat in a report stands out.

Ask for a diagram, or type /diagram and what to draw, and Graft draws it with the built-in diagram-design skill: architecture, flows, sequences, data models and forty more kinds, laid out by hand rather than by a layout engine. The diagram appears in the conversation when the turn ends.
A diagram opens large with zoom, copies to the clipboard as a picture, and saves as PNG or SVG. The file itself is an ordinary .html page in your project that any browser opens.
Chats draw diagrams too, and keep them with the chat’s files.
Customize → Skills shows the skills that come with Graft. A skill of your own with the same name replaces one.
Reading a skill’s own files no longer asks for permission.
Previews of pages have Geist, Geist Mono and Instrument Serif without a network.
This build holds three rounds of work in one: the session view and checked edits of 0.6.17, the tool journal and MCP permissions of 0.6.22, and diagrams. Their notes are below.

After a crash, a forced quit or a power cut, the agent is told the truth about what it was doing. A command that had started has an unknown outcome and is checked before it is repeated; one that had finished keeps its result; one that never started is said not to have run. A note in the session says what was cut off. Before, all of it was reported as "not run".

A reply that arrives damaged no longer has its commands run. When part of a model's reply is lost on the way, what is left of a command can still look complete and mean something else, so the agent is asked again and the reply is marked as possibly incomplete.
Stop works even when a tool ignores it: after two seconds the turn goes on without it and says the tool may still be finishing.
Quitting can no longer hang. Each part of shutting down has a time limit, and one that fails no longer leaves your commands running.

Integrations: every tool of an MCP server has a permission of its own (Default, Always ask, Allow, Never), and so does the server as a whole. A tool's "read-only" label is the server's own word; your choice is not.

Integrations: choose what a local MCP server gets from your computer's environment. New servers start without your keys, tokens and passwords; servers you already have keep what they had until you change it.
Limits for one turn: two more, tool calls and retries, and all six now have a group of their own in Settings → Permissions.
The agent can ask what a change to a file can reach: every file that imports it, directly or through others, and the tests among them, the nearest first.
A turn that changed files in a project with no checks says so once, and names the checks the project could have.

Code sessions keep what Graft says in view. The steps between fold into one line that opens into a list, such as “Read 2 files” or “Created a file, edited 5 files +185 −9”, and a running turn shows the step in progress with the time so far. Your messages sit on the right. Pick Normal, Thinking, Verbose or the earlier one-line Summary from the eye under the message box, or in Settings → Appearance.
Commands read in the tense that fits: “Running the unit tests” while they run, “Ran the unit tests” afterwards.
Diffs mark the words that changed inside a line and take syntax colours, in the transcript and in the Changes panel. An edit’s diff names its file.

In a trusted TypeScript or JavaScript project Graft finds a declaration by its name alone, then every use of it, the classes that implement an interface, and where the type of a value is declared, all from the built-in language server instead of by searching text. The transcript says what it looked up.

After Graft edits a TypeScript or JavaScript file in a trusted project with its packages installed, the built-in language server checks that file and Graft sees its errors with the edit’s result, so it fixes them in its next step. The transcript lists them under the diff. An edit waits at most five seconds for its check. Settings → Models → Check edits for errors turns this off.

API keys, tokens and passwords in command output, tool output and diffs are covered until you press the eye beside them. What is stored, and what the model reads, is unchanged. A change you are asked to approve is shown as it is.
The “Edited files” card of the last turn has Undo. It opens the rewind dialog on Files only, with the files that would change.

Settings has a search box. Type a word and it finds the setting on whichever page it is, and says which; Enter opens the first one, and the setting shows itself on its page. The pages are listed under headings: You, Models, Agent, App and Data.
What you were typing survives a restart (never for incognito chats). A session opens where you left it scrolled. The permission-mode menu takes number keys.
Fixed: a long line in a diff or in command output could stretch the transcript sideways. It now scrolls inside its own box.

A stopped or timed-out command no longer leaves processes behind. On Windows, what Git Bash started is ended even when its own parent had already exited, and if that list can't be read the command itself is still stopped. On macOS and Linux, a child that ignores the first signal is ended two seconds later.
A reply from Claude or Gemini that breaks off mid-stream is reported as an error instead of passing for a finished reply, and its tool calls are not run. What had already arrived stays on screen.

Pages that Graft shows but did not write are granted no permissions. The hidden window that takes pictures of your sites could be granted location or notifications without asking; every such window now starts with everything refused.
Editor: Ctrl+S pressed right after typing always saves, and saves everything you typed. Before, that save could be skipped without a word, or write a draft a few letters short.

Usage: Settings → Usage shows what Graft used on each day and with each model: requests, tokens sent and written, and what it cost. Counting starts with this version. A model with no published price is counted without a cost, and incognito chats are not counted.

Limits for one turn: Settings → Permissions can pause a turn after a number of tokens, an estimated cost, or minutes of work, counting the agents the turn starts. The pause says which limit was reached and offers to continue. The cost is worked out from published prices, so your bill can differ, and a model with no published price is named when it answers. No limit is set until you set one.
The backup model also finishes the work of a sub-agent, or of an agent in a group, when that agent's model keeps failing. The agent's record says which model took over and why.
Gemini 3 and later are told how hard to think by level, as Google's API asks, and the effort menu shows the levels each model has. Earlier Gemini models keep their thinking budget.

Chats have the / menu: /research, /context, /clear, /compact and the other commands a chat can use. /model opens the chat's model menu. Commands that work on a project, such as /plan, /commit and /review, say so in a chat instead of being sent to the model.
With only / typed, the menu lists every command instead of the twelve with the shortest names, and the list follows the arrow keys as you move through it.
A project whose only session is listed under Needs you keeps its header in the sidebar, with the button to start another session there.
Smoother transitions for controls, queued messages and loading states. Reduced motion now removes entrance delays too; status clocks pause while the app is hidden.
Long conversations reuse completed transcript turns while a reply streams, reducing repeated processing without dropping conversation history.
Keep several files open in tabs. Tab paths and editing modes survive restart; switching or closing a tab retains unsaved drafts for recovery.
In trusted TypeScript and JavaScript projects, References and Symbol info show real language-server results for the current draft. Shift+F12 finds references; F12 still opens definitions.
Responses containing repeated model control tokens show endpoint troubleshooting guidance while preserving the original output. Normal multilingual text and code examples remain unchanged.

Interrupted provider streams fail safely before tool execution. Already-visible partial thinking and text are retained, and late session loads cannot overwrite newer messages, approvals or queue state.

Edit project files in the Files panel with Monaco. Ctrl/Cmd+S checks the disk revision before saving, and unsaved drafts are backed up on this device for recovery after restarting. External changes keep your draft and require review.

Local TypeScript and JavaScript intelligence: agents can query definitions, references, types, outlines and diagnostics. In a trusted project, Check types checks the editor draft and F12 opens its definition.

Model metadata updates independently of app updates. Settings → Providers has automatic refresh controls, offline fallback and refresh status. Missing models and connection failures retain metadata without silently changing your selected model.

Native OpenAI shutdown announcements show the date and prevent selecting models after their dated UTC day has passed. Pick replacements explicitly; a missing catalog entry alone cannot confirm retirement.

Writing group agents and writing Tasks work in private checkouts. Successful patches integrate only if destination files still match; conflicts retain a checkout and patch with recovery details in the Agents panel.

Reliability fixes preserve context pruning across restarts, protect file-tool revisions, respect Retry-After, strengthen credential redaction and prevent preview-server connections from holding up shutdown. Targeted dependency fixes include the editor’s embedded sanitizer.
Needs you: sessions that wait for an answer or an approval, or stopped with an error, are listed at the top of the sidebar. The session you have open stays in its place.

See what fills the context. Type /context, or click the context ring: the system prompt, tools, your messages, replies, tool results and reasoning, each with its size. They are estimates from the text, shown next to the provider's own count.
Notifications have a sound switch (Settings → Notifications). A finished session stays quiet either way.
A rewind to before a summary, or to before /clear, brings the earlier conversation back for the model. Before, those messages stayed on screen but were no longer sent.

Models on Ollama are measured against the context Graft asks Ollama for: 32K, or the size you set for the model in Settings → Models. Before, Graft counted against the size the model was trained for while Ollama kept only 32K and dropped older messages without saying so. Models that Ollama passes on to a hosted service get their whole window.

Long sessions last longer. When the context fills up, Graft first drops the output of old tool calls, which the agent can run again, and only summarizes when that is not enough. The transcript still shows everything.
A summary no longer starts the agent from scratch: the latest steps stay exactly as they were, after the summary of what came before.
A backup model. Choose one in Settings → Models, and when a session's model is overloaded, rate limited or unreachable after its retries, the turn continues on the backup and says so.
The plan card in the transcript shows the plan you approved. After an edit it showed the plan as first offered under “Approved”; it now shows your version and says “Approved with your changes”.
Edit a plan before you approve it. The approval card has Edit plan: change the steps, and the agent follows your version.
The plan stays. Once approved it sits above the message box with how many tasks are done, opens with a click, and is repeated word for word when a long conversation is compacted.

/plan and what you want planned switches to Plan mode and asks for a plan. Plans now come as a goal, steps with the files they touch, the checks that will prove it, and the risks; when a request leaves a real choice open, the agent asks first.

Research: type /research and a question. Graft plans the questions to answer, searches, opens the pages instead of trusting excerpts, checks claims against a second source and writes a report with its sources. It works in chats and in code sessions.
Chats can run several researchers at once, each on one part of a question, and bring their findings back together. They can search and read the web and nothing else.

You can see what an answer stands on. A reply that read pages ends with the list of them, and a cited link says whether the page was opened, only found by a search, or neither: those have a dashed border. Pages a researcher opened count, and so does a page that answered from another address than the one asked for.
A chat asks before it reads a page on this computer or your local network, and a page on the web can no longer send Graft there with a redirect.
Reading a server on this computer by name (http://localhost:…) works whichever kind of address it listens on. Before, a dev server that listened on one kind only could fail with “fetch failed”.

Chats make real documents. Ask for a PDF, a text document (.docx), slides (.pptx) or a spreadsheet (.xlsx) and Graft builds it from what the model writes, with headings, lists, tables, links and the pictures made in that chat. Each one appears as a card to save, open or show in its folder.

A document is built inside Graft, in a window that runs no script and loads nothing from the web. Spreadsheets take numbers and formulas, on one sheet or several; slides take a title, bullets, a table, a picture and speaker’s notes. A formula that would reach outside the workbook stays text, and Graft only saves office files it built itself.

Models show their real context size. A provider added by typing its address used to give every model 32K, even ones with a million tokens. Graft now recognises the address, believes what the server reports about its own models, and otherwise uses the size most providers give for a model of that name. A size nothing vouches for is marked “assumed”, a 128,000-token model no longer reads “125K”, and a session’s context ring follows the model you picked instead of the size recorded at its last turn.
If a server refuses the reply length its catalog entry suggests, Graft retries with what the server allows instead of failing the request.
The files card shows what each file is: a document, a spreadsheet, slides, a picture, a web page or code.

Agents can write side by side. Give each agent its own files or folders and they work at the same time, each kept to its own paths and reading a file itself before it changes it; an agent with no paths of its own still works alone. The Agents panel shows who may change what.

Faster turns. When the agent asks for several things at once, neighbouring reads and searches run together even with an edit among them, and every step still sees what came before it. A reply that fills the model’s context window now makes room and carries on instead of stopping.

OpenAI’s -pro, Codex and deep-research models work. They are only served by OpenAI’s Responses API, which Graft now speaks, with a summary of their reasoning shown as they think; the Codex models are in the model list too. This is tested against recordings of the API, not against a live account.

The model catalog is refreshed from models.dev: 212 providers and 7,553 models, including the newest Claude, Gemini, Grok, GLM, Qwen and DeepSeek releases. What a model costs and can do comes from it and from each provider’s own list.

MCP does more than tools. Graft passes on what a server says about using itself (marked as the server’s words, never as rules), lets the agent list and read the resources a server publishes, offers its prompts as /mcp__server__prompt commands, shows results that are only structured data, and tells programs running on this computer which project folders are open. A setup with many tools (GitHub’s alone has dozens) no longer weighs on every request: the agent finds and loads what it needs with a search, and the prompt says which servers are waiting.
When an edit misses, the error shows the lines the file really has at the nearest match, so the agent can fix it without reading the file again.

Pictures show in the Files panel. Click an image and you see it, with its size in pixels, instead of “Too large to preview” or “Binary file”; switch between fitting the panel and its actual size. Clips and sound play there too, and an SVG shows as the picture or as its source.

Every file and folder has a menu, from its … button or a right-click: copy its path, copy its path within the project, copy a picture itself to paste elsewhere, show it in its folder, open it with its own app or in your editor, or add it to your message. The preview keeps Copy path and Show in folder one click away. Scripts and programs are never opened by a click.
When the agent reads a picture, the step in the conversation now shows the picture, with the same actions, instead of the word “Image”.

Agents: for work that splits up, Graft can run a group of agents, such as explorers side by side, then an implementer, a tester and reviewers. Each one gets a role, a context of its own, its own model, a time limit and (if you set one) a token budget, and can be given a command that has to pass before its work counts. The new Agents panel draws the group as a graph while it runs: click an agent to see its model and why it was chosen, its tools, the files it changed, tokens, cost, report, failed attempts and every step, or to stop just that one. Settings → Models → Agents chooses a model for each kind of work.

Missions: type /mission, give an objective, say what done means and list the commands that must pass. Graft then keeps working turn after turn and keeps a notebook of what it finds and decides. It counts the mission as done only when your commands pass; a failed one goes back to the agent with its output. A mission pauses when you stop it, when the agent needs something only you can give, or at its turn limit, and it is still there after a restart.

Generated images: when you ask for them, Graft makes pictures for a site or a project with an image model from OpenRouter, OpenAI or Gemini, or with your own ComfyUI, including the workflows you saved and video nodes if you have them. Set it up in Settings → Images. Nothing is generated unless you ask, and what each picture cost is shown.

The agent sees how the code fits together: one step now answers where a name is defined, every file that uses it, what imports a file and which tests cover it, in JavaScript and TypeScript, Python, Go, Rust, Java, Kotlin, C#, C and C++, Ruby, PHP and Swift.

Reverse engineering: a Ghidra integration (Settings → Integrations) to import and decompile programs, and /decompile, which rebuilds compiled code one function at a time and counts a function only when the project’s own check says it matches.

Motion: menus, dialogs, panels and steps open and close with short, quiet animations, and replies stream in smoothly instead of in bursts; long replies no longer slow the app down. Settings → Appearance → Motion chooses System, On or Reduced, and On works even when Windows has animations turned off.
Fixes: a finished reply no longer jumps while checks run after it, and each settings page opens at its top instead of where the last one was scrolled to.

Edits land more often, especially with local and smaller models. When a model quotes the right lines with the wrong indentation (tabs read as spaces, a block one level off), Graft now finds the one block with that text, makes the change and fits the new lines to the file’s indentation, instead of sending the model back to read the file again. It never guesses between two candidates, and the diff you approve shows exactly what will change.

A conversation that outgrows the model no longer ends the turn. When a provider refuses a request as too long (common with custom endpoints and local models, where the real limit is unknown or smaller than listed), Graft summarizes the conversation and sends the request again. It does this when “compact automatically” is on.

Building a site no longer freezes Graft. On PCs where Windows Security’s Controlled folder access protects Documents, Windows blocked the new site’s folder and Graft waited forever. New sites now go in a Graft Sites folder in your user folder, which Windows doesn’t lock and OneDrive doesn’t sync; sites already in Documents › Graft Sites stay there.
When Windows won’t let Graft create or change a file, Graft and the agent now say so and how to allow it, instead of hanging or reporting “no such file or directory”.

Sites: describe a website and Graft designs and builds it, then hosts it on your computer at its own address (like peach-palace.localhost) with a live preview that reloads as it changes. The Sites tab keeps a gallery of them with previews, and each is a folder in Documents › Graft Sites, ready to publish anywhere.

Connected apps work properly: Roblox Studio tools that appear after it connects now show up, servers that start empty are asked again, long jobs that report progress (a render, a download) are no longer cut off after two minutes, apps started with npx or uvx get your full environment, older HTTP servers work, and a server that crashes reconnects. When Blender, Roblox Studio or Unity isn’t ready, Graft says what to check.
Chats can use your connected apps too, asking before each action.
Taproot grows a root: picking the deepest effort turns the slider into a living leaf-to-gold gradient, draws a small root and says what it costs.

Computer use is easier to follow: a ring marks each click, the banner says what the agent is doing, each step shows its screenshot in the chat, and the agent can zoom in to read small text or open an app by name.
Fixes: a moved or deleted project folder no longer shows as “Git is not installed”, Git is found even when it isn’t on PATH, and session titles work for people using free models with no credits.

Checks after changes: list your project’s checks (type check, lint, tests) in Customize → Checks and Graft runs them after every turn that changed files. When one fails, the agent gets the output and fixes the cause, up to two rounds. Graft suggests the commands from your package.json, Cargo, Go or Python setup.

A sandbox for code you don’t trust: turn it on for a project and its commands run in a Docker or Podman container that sees only the project folder. Your other files, keys, credentials and environment variables stay out of reach, .git and .graft are read-only inside it, and one switch cuts off the network. In Auto-edit and Auto, sandboxed commands run without asking.

A better Browser panel: a console with an error badge, find in page, zoom, phone and tablet widths, developer tools, reload without cache and clearing site data. Send a screenshot, a picked element or the console straight into your message. With no page open it lists the dev servers running on your computer.
The agent can test web apps: it opens your dev server in the Browser panel, clicks and types like a person, reads the console and takes screenshots.
Fixes: Stop now clears a waiting approval or question, the changes panel works for sessions in a subfolder of a repository, and a session list that fails to load offers a retry.

Integrations: connect Blender, Roblox Studio, Unity, Godot, Figma, a Playwright browser, GitHub, Context7, Sentry, Linear and Notion from Settings → Integrations. Graft checks what each one needs on your computer, shows the setup steps and adds it in one click.
Tokens you give an integration are kept encrypted with your system keyring, not in a settings file.
The command palette matches what you type more precisely: letters scattered across a long command no longer count as a match.
Long tasks no longer stop at 150 steps: a turn runs until the work is done. You can still set a limit in Settings → Permissions, and a turn that reaches it pauses with a Continue button.
A command palette: press Ctrl+Shift+P, or type > in search, to run almost anything. Start sessions, switch palettes and themes, open any settings page, export, compact or rewind.

Settings → Personalization tells Graft about you and how you like answers, with a response style (balanced, concise, explanatory or learning) and your own instructions. Chats and code sessions use it; incognito chats never do.
Rewritten instructions for chats and code sessions, and View system prompt (session menu or /system) shows exactly what Graft sends to the model.
Six colour palettes, each light and dark (Graft, Midnight, Slate, Grove, Dune and High contrast), seven accent colours, and smoother motion throughout.
Start a message with ! in a code session to run a shell command yourself, such as !npm test; Graft sees the output with your next message. ↑ and ↓ bring back messages you sent.
Custom agents: make specialists such as a reviewer, a test writer or a debugger in Customize → Agents, and Graft hands them tasks.
New commands: /commit, /pr, /security-review, /explain, /test, /export, /system and /new. A command file of your own can replace any of the prompt commands.
Messages you type while Graft works can go right away: Send now hands one over after the current step without stopping anything. Queued messages can also be edited or removed, in chats too.
Scion the sprout comes alive: it blinks, looks around and wiggles its leaves, flaps them while Graft works, and hops when you hover over it or click it.

Updates work again. Every earlier version failed its update check (“Cannot set properties of undefined”), so install this one by hand once; from here on Graft downloads new versions itself and asks to restart.
If an update check ever fails, Settings → About links straight to the releases page so you can download the newest installer yourself.
A copy of Graft that can’t update itself now says so instead of showing “Checking for updates…” forever.
Chats can make files for you to download (documents, data, code, pictures) and run JavaScript in a locked-down sandbox for calculations and data work.
Chats know the time: each message carries when it was sent, so “what time is it?” gets a real answer.

Read aloud can pause, resume and stop, and sounds far more natural with OpenRouter’s voices (Kokoro by default, about $0.0006 per 1,000 characters). Pick the voice and speed in Settings → Voice; incognito chats always use your computer’s voice.
Taproot answers questions and quick requests directly instead of planning and reviewing work that never happened.
Free web search with no key or account: Exa by default, and DuckDuckGo when Exa is busy. Searching no longer costs anything unless you pick a paid engine.
The engine you pick in Settings → Web search now decides every search; Claude’s built-in search runs only when you pick Anthropic.
Site icons load for far more sites, YouTube and npm among them, and a site without one shows a globe instead of a letter.
On Windows, the taskbar shows Graft’s own icon and name instead of Electron’s.
Web search in chats and code sessions through your own provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini or OpenRouter), or Brave, Tavily or SearXNG, with site chips while it searches and cited sources as pills.
Each turn’s work folds into one line with a live status while it runs, and an “Edited N files” card lists every change with its diff.
Taproot now investigates, plans with a task list it has to finish, verifies with real checks and reviews its own diff before reporting.
Computer use on Windows (opt-in in Settings → Permissions): the agent can see the screen and use the mouse and keyboard, asking first, and Ctrl+Alt+Esc stops it.
Updates from GitHub releases, with a prompt to restart when one is ready; a transcript width setting; faster startup.
Checkpoints and rewind work with older Git versions too, including the one macOS ships, and Linux builds come as an AppImage and a .deb.
Meet Scion: the pixel sprout is now Graft’s icon in the taskbar, the tray and the installer, and its mark inside the app.
Over 200 providers from an open model catalog, with a searchable picker, per-model effort levels and accurate costs.
Settings → Privacy: ask providers not to train on your data, and incognito chats that stay off your computer.
A real Bypass mode you switch on in Settings, plus Files and “Keep computer awake” in the session menu.
Prompt caching for Claude models on OpenRouter, and session spend in the context popover.
Code sessions with a real agent loop: read, edit, search, run commands and fetch pages, with a permission prompt for anything risky.
Five permission modes, including Plan (read-only until you approve a plan) and Auto (low-risk actions run without asking).
Git worktrees per session, hidden checkpoints before every turn, and rewind for files, conversation or both.
Works with Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, OpenRouter, Ollama and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
Taproot: a long-horizon effort mode that keeps going until the work is verified.
